# Task 4: Building a Greenlight Risk Model

## Data Preparation

```{r}
#| label: task1-setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

focus_genres <- c(
  "Action", "Comedy", "Drama",
  "Horror", "Animation"
)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year),
         release_year <= 2016) |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget < 10000, NA_real_, 
                     as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue <= 0, NA_real_,
                      as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = if_else(
      !is.na(budget) & !is.na(revenue),
      revenue / budget,
      NA_real_
    ),
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )

movies_focus <- movies_clean |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% focus_genres)
```


## Introduction

This analysis examines whether information available before production can help Meridian identify films at risk of failing to recover their budgets. Frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models were fitted using genre, franchise status, budget and crew size. The results are used to assess classification performance and estimate financial risk for three hypothetical film proposals.

## Outcome and Predictor Definitions

```{r}
#| label: task4-outcome
#| include: false

# movies_clean was created in the shared setup chunk.

task4_data <- movies_clean |>
  mutate(
    flop = case_when(
      is.na(roi) ~ NA_integer_,
      roi < 1 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L      
    )
  )

# Check the outcome categories.
task4_data |>
  count(flop, name = "number_of_films")
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-data-checks
#| include: false

# Check missing values in the selected predictors.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    missing_genre = sum(is.na(primary_genre)),
    missing_franchise = sum(is.na(franchise_status)),
    missing_budget = sum(is.na(budget_m)),
    missing_crew = sum(is.na(crew_size))
  )

# Count films with complete information for modelling.
task4_data |>
  summarise(
    complete_model_cases = sum(
      complete.cases(
        flop,
        primary_genre,
        franchise_status,
        budget_m,
        crew_size
      )
    )
  )
```

Financial risk was assessed using return on investment (ROI), calculated as box-office revenue divided by production budget. A film was classified as a *flop* when its ROI was below 1, indicating that reported revenue did not recover the production budget. Films with an ROI of 1 or higher were classified as *non-flops*, while those with missing ROI were left unclassified.

Of the 4,801 films examined, 785 were identified as flops and 2,429 as non-flops, with the remaining 1,587 lacking sufficient financial information for classification. Among the 3,214 films with known outcomes, the observed flop rate was approximately 24.4%.

Logistic regression was selected because the outcome is binary, allowing the model to estimate the probability of a film flopping while keeping predicted values between 0 and 1. Linear regression is less appropriate because its predictions are not restricted to this range, whereas Poisson regression is primarily designed for count outcomes rather than binary classifications.

The proposed predictors were primary genre, franchise status, production budget and crew size, as these characteristics can reasonably be considered before a film receives production approval. After accounting for missing outcome and predictor information, 3,213 films had complete observations available for modelling. However, the substantial amount of missing financial data remains an important limitation, as films with recorded outcomes may not be representative of the wider dataset, potentially introducing selection bias.

## Frequentist Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-initial-model
#| include: false

task4_initial_model <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_m + crew_size,
  data = task4_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_initial_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-genre-diagnostic
#| include: false

task4_data |>
  filter(!is.na(flop), !is.na(primary_genre)) |>
  count(primary_genre, flop) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = flop,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "flop_"
  ) |>
  mutate(total = flop_0 + flop_1) |>
  arrange(total)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-data
#| include: false

task4_model_data <- task4_data |>
  mutate(
    budget_10m = budget_m / 10,
    crew_10 = crew_size / 10
  ) |>
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      flop,
      primary_genre,
      franchise_status,
      budget_10m,
      crew_10
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-model
#| include: false

task4_frequentist <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_10m + crew_10,
  data = task4_model_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(task4_frequentist)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-odds
#| include: false

odds_ratios <- exp(coef(task4_frequentist))

wald_intervals <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

task4_odds_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(odds_ratios),
  Odds_Ratio = odds_ratios,
  CI_Lower = exp(wald_intervals[, 1]),
  CI_Upper = exp(wald_intervals[, 2])
)

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  print(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-frequentist-results
#| echo: false

task4_odds_table |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Predictor %in% c(
      "franchise_statusFranchise",
      "budget_10m",
      "crew_10"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(
      Predictor,
      franchise_statusFranchise = "Franchise (vs original)",
      budget_10m = "Budget (+$10 million)",
      crew_10 = "Crew (+10 members)"
    ),
    dplyr::across(
      c(Odds_Ratio, CI_Lower, CI_Upper),
      ~ round(.x, 3)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor",
      "Odds ratio",
      "95% CI lower",
      "95% CI upper"
    ),
    caption = "Selected frequentist logistic regression results"
  )
```
**Interpretation**

The frequentist logistic regression was fitted using 3,213 films with complete information. After accounting for genre, budget and crew size, franchise films had approximately 77.6% lower odds of flopping than original films (OR = 0.224, 95% CI: 0.126–0.399). A further $10 million in budget was associated with 4.0% lower odds of flopping (OR = 0.960, 95% CI: 0.936–0.985), while an additional 10 crew members was associated with 9.4% lower odds (OR = 0.906, 95% CI: 0.877–0.936). These findings suggest that franchise status, budget and crew size are associated with financial outcomes, although they do not establish causal relationships.

**Limitations**

The model has two important limitations. First, the Foreign genre contained only one film with a known outcome, which was a flop. This resulted in complete separation and an unstable coefficient, making its estimated odds ratio unreliable. Second, the analysis used 3,213 of the original 4,801 films because observations with missing information were excluded. If missing financial data are not random, the estimated relationships may not represent all films. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results and comparing them with the Bayesian model.

## Bayesian Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-data-checks
#| include: false

# Outcome balance
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::count(flop) |>
  dplyr::mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))

# Number of flops and non-flops in each genre
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::group_by(primary_genre) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    films = dplyr::n(),
    flops = sum(flop == 1),
    non_flops = sum(flop == 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(films)

# Predictor scales
task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    budget_sd = sd(budget_10m),
    crew_sd = sd(crew_10),
    budget_median = median(budget_10m),
    crew_median = median(crew_10),
    budget_max = max(budget_10m),
    crew_max = max(crew_10)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-predictors
#| include: false

task4_budget_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$budget_10m)
task4_budget_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$budget_10m)

task4_crew_mean <- mean(task4_model_data$crew_10)
task4_crew_sd <- sd(task4_model_data$crew_10)

task4_bayesian_data <- task4_model_data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    budget_z = (budget_10m - task4_budget_mean) /
      task4_budget_sd,
    crew_z = (crew_10 - task4_crew_mean) /
      task4_crew_sd
  )

summary(task4_bayesian_data[, c("budget_z", "crew_z")])
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-check
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

# Draw hypothetical coefficients from proposed priors
prior_intercept <- 2.5 * rt(10000, df = 3)
prior_franchise <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
prior_budget <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
prior_crew <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)

# Illustrative profile: original film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_original <- plogis(prior_intercept)

# Illustrative profile: franchise film with average budget and crew
prior_prob_franchise <- plogis(
  prior_intercept + prior_franchise
)

# Summarise implied prior probabilities
rbind(
  Original = quantile(
    prior_prob_original,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  ),
  Franchise = quantile(
    prior_prob_franchise,
    c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-comparison
#| include: false

set.seed(2420)

n_draws <- 10000

# Candidate intercept priors
intercept_a <- 2.5 * rt(n_draws, df = 3)
intercept_b <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = -1, sd = 1)

# Other coefficient priors
franchise_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 1.5)
budget_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)
crew_effect <- rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5)

# Representative profiles on standardised scales
prior_profiles <- data.frame(
  profile = c(
    "Original, average scale",
    "Franchise, average scale",
    "Original, higher scale"
  ),
  franchise = c(0, 1, 0),
  budget_z = c(0, 0, 1),
  crew_z = c(0, 0, 1)
)

# Function to summarise implied probabilities
check_prior <- function(intercept, prior_name) {

  results <- lapply(
    seq_len(nrow(prior_profiles)),
    function(i) {

      log_odds <- intercept +
        franchise_effect * prior_profiles$franchise[i] +
        budget_effect * prior_profiles$budget_z[i] +
        crew_effect * prior_profiles$crew_z[i]

      probabilities <- plogis(log_odds)

      data.frame(
        prior = prior_name,
        profile = prior_profiles$profile[i],
        lower = quantile(probabilities, 0.025),
        median = median(probabilities),
        upper = quantile(probabilities, 0.975)
      )
    }
  )

  dplyr::bind_rows(results)
}

prior_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  check_prior(intercept_a, "A: Student-t(3, 0, 2.5)"),
  check_prior(intercept_b, "B: Normal(-1, 1)")
)

print(prior_comparison)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-final-priors
#| include: false

# Design matrix for Bayesian logistic regression
task4_formula <- flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status +
  budget_z + crew_z

task4_X <- model.matrix(
  task4_formula,
  data = task4_bayesian_data
)

task4_y <- task4_bayesian_data$flop

# Prior standard deviations for regression coefficients
task4_prior_sd <- rep(1.5, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_sd) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_sd["(Intercept)"] <- 1
task4_prior_sd["budget_z"] <- 0.5
task4_prior_sd["crew_z"] <- 0.5

# Prior means
task4_prior_mean <- rep(0, ncol(task4_X))
names(task4_prior_mean) <- colnames(task4_X)

task4_prior_mean["(Intercept)"] <- -1

# Log-posterior = log-likelihood + log-prior
task4_log_posterior <- function(beta) {

  eta <- drop(task4_X %*% beta)

  # Numerically stable Bernoulli log-likelihood
  log_likelihood <- sum(
    task4_y * eta -
      (pmax(eta, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(eta))))
  )

  log_prior <- sum(
    dnorm(
      beta,
      mean = task4_prior_mean,
      sd = task4_prior_sd,
      log = TRUE
    )
  )

  log_likelihood + log_prior
}
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-prior-predictive
#| include: false
#| eval: false

task4_prior_fit <- brms::brm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status +
    budget_z + crew_z,
  data = task4_bayesian_data,
  family = brms::bernoulli(),
  prior = task4_bayesian_priors,
  sample_prior = "only",
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  chains = 2,
  iter = 1000,
  warmup = 500,
  cores = 2,
  seed = 2420,
  file = "task4_prior_predictive_fit"
)

# Prior-predictive probabilities for all modelled films
prior_probabilities <- brms::posterior_epred(
  task4_prior_fit
)

# Distribution of the average implied flop probability
prior_average_risk <- rowMeans(prior_probabilities)

quantile(
  prior_average_risk,
  c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
)

# Simulated number of flops in the modelling sample
prior_simulated_outcomes <- brms::posterior_predict(
  task4_prior_fit
)

prior_flop_counts <- rowSums(prior_simulated_outcomes)

quantile(
  prior_flop_counts,
  c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-fit
#| include: false

# Locate a suitable starting point for Metropolis sampling
task4_mode <- optim(
  par = task4_prior_mean,
  fn = function(beta) -task4_log_posterior(beta),
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000)
)

print(task4_mode$convergence)

# Estimate the proposal covariance
task4_proposal_cov <- solve(task4_mode$hessian)

# Run four Metropolis-Hastings chains
set.seed(2420)

task4_mh_chains <- lapply(1:4, function(chain) {

  starting_values <- as.numeric(
    MASS::mvrnorm(
      1,
      mu = task4_mode$par,
      Sigma = task4_proposal_cov
    )
  )

  chain_result <- MCMCpack::MCMCmetrop1R(
    fun = task4_log_posterior,
    theta.init = starting_values,
    V = task4_proposal_cov,
    tune = 0.4,
    burnin = 4000,
    mcmc = 12000,
    thin = 1,
    logfun = TRUE,
    verbose = 0
  )

  colnames(chain_result) <- colnames(task4_X)

  chain_result
})

task4_mh_chains <- do.call(
  coda::mcmc.list,
  task4_mh_chains
)
saveRDS(task4_mh_chains, "task4_mh_fit.rds")

# Combine the four chains into a matrix of posterior draws
task4_mh_draws <- as.matrix(task4_mh_chains)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-bayesian-diagnostics
#| include: false

# Check agreement between the four chains
task4_rhat <- coda::gelman.diag(
  task4_mh_chains,
  multivariate = FALSE
)

# Check effective sample sizes
task4_ess <- coda::effectiveSize(task4_mh_chains)

print(task4_rhat)
cat("Minimum ESS:", round(min(task4_ess), 1), "\n")
cat(
  "Maximum upper R-hat:",
  round(max(task4_rhat$psrf[, 2]), 3),
  "\n"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-bayesian-results
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Selected Bayesian logistic regression estimates with 95% credible intervals."

task4_bayesian_results <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Franchise (vs original)",
    "Budget (+$10 million)",
    "Crew (+10 members)"
  ),
  Median_OR = c(
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"])),
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd)),
    median(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd))
  ),
  Lower = c(
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]), 0.025),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd), 0.025),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd), 0.025)
  ),
  Upper = c(
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]), 0.975),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd), 0.975),
    quantile(exp(task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd), 0.975)
  )
)

task4_bayesian_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Median odds ratio (95% CrI)` = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.3f–%.3f)", Median_OR, Lower, Upper
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(Predictor, `Median odds ratio (95% CrI)`) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

**Bayesian findings and limitations**

The Bayesian logistic regression was estimated using four Metropolis–Hastings chains. The acceptance rates were approximately 35.5%–36.6%, with a minimum effective sample size of 522.1 and a maximum upper R-hat of 1.012. These diagnostics suggest that the chains mixed reasonably well and produced sufficiently consistent estimates for the main analysis.

The Bayesian results were broadly consistent with the frequentist model. Franchise films had lower estimated flop odds than original films, while higher budgets and larger crews were also associated with lower flop odds. These are associations rather than evidence of causation.

The Foreign genre requires particular caution. Only one film in this category had a known outcome, making its estimated effect highly uncertain. Its posterior median coefficient was 0.939, with a 95% credible interval from −1.186 to 3.413 on the log-odds scale. Since this interval includes zero, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether this genre has higher or lower flop odds than the reference genre. The Bayesian prior helped stabilise the estimate, but it cannot compensate for the lack of observations.

## Model Comparison

```{r}
#| label: task4-model-comparison-data
#| include: false

# Frequentist estimates
frequentist_coefs <- coef(task4_frequentist)
frequentist_ci <- confint.default(task4_frequentist)

predictors <- c(
  "franchise_statusFranchise",
  "budget_10m",
  "crew_10"
)


# Convert Bayesian coefficients to comparable odds ratios
bayesian_or_draws <- cbind(
  Franchise = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]
  ),
  Budget = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "budget_z"] / task4_budget_sd
  ),
  Crew = exp(
    task4_mh_draws[, "crew_z"] / task4_crew_sd
  )
)

# Summarise posterior odds ratios
bayesian_medians <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, median)
bayesian_lower <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, quantile, 0.025)
bayesian_upper <- apply(bayesian_or_draws, 2, quantile, 0.975)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Franchise", "Budget (+$10m)", "Crew (+10)"),
  Frequentist_OR = exp(frequentist_coefs[predictors]),
  Frequentist_Lower = exp(frequentist_ci[predictors, 1]),
  Frequentist_Upper = exp(frequentist_ci[predictors, 2]),
  Bayesian_OR = as.numeric(bayesian_medians),
  Bayesian_Lower = as.numeric(bayesian_lower),
  Bayesian_Upper = as.numeric(bayesian_upper)
)

print(comparison)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-model-comparison

  ),

knitr::kable(
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-posterior-probability
#| include: false

# Posterior probability that franchise status reduces flop odds
franchise_draws <- task4_mh_draws[, "franchise_statusFranchise"]

prob_franchise_negative <- mean(franchise_draws < 0)

print(prob_franchise_negative)
```

The frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models produced closely aligned results. Franchise films had lower estimated odds of flopping than original films, with a frequentist odds ratio of 0.224 (95% CI: 0.126–0.399) and a Bayesian odds ratio of 0.238 (95% CrI: 0.132–0.390). Budget and crew size also showed similar negative associations with flop odds across both models.

Although the intervals are numerically similar, their interpretations differ. A frequentist 95% confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of the estimation method, whereas a Bayesian 95% credible interval describes uncertainty about the parameter given the data, model and priors.

All retained Metropolis–Hastings samples for the franchise coefficient were negative, giving an estimated posterior probability above 99.9% that franchise status is associated with lower flop odds after accounting for genre, budget and crew size. However, neither approach establishes a causal relationship.

## Classification Performance

```{r}
#| label: task4-classification-predictions
#| include: false

# Predict flop probabilities using the frequentist model
task4_predicted_prob <- predict(
  task4_frequentist,
  newdata = task4_model_data,
  type = "response"
)

# Classify films using a 50% probability threshold
task4_predicted_class <- ifelse(
  task4_predicted_prob >= 0.5,
  1L,
  0L
)

# Compare predicted and actual outcomes
task4_confusion <- table(
  Actual = factor(task4_model_data$flop, levels = c(0, 1)),
  Predicted = factor(task4_predicted_class, levels = c(0, 1))
)

print(task4_confusion)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-classification-metrics
#| include: false

# Extract the four confusion matrix counts
task4_tn <- task4_confusion["0", "0"]
task4_fp <- task4_confusion["0", "1"]
task4_fn <- task4_confusion["1", "0"]
task4_tp <- task4_confusion["1", "1"]

# Calculate classification performance
task4_accuracy <- (task4_tp + task4_tn) / sum(task4_confusion)

task4_sensitivity <- task4_tp / (task4_tp + task4_fn)

task4_specificity <- task4_tn / (task4_tn + task4_fp)

task4_precision <- if (
  task4_tp + task4_fp > 0
) {
  task4_tp / (task4_tp + task4_fp)
} else {
  NA_real_
}

# Summarise performance
task4_metrics <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Accuracy",
    "Sensitivity (flops)",
    "Specificity (non-flops)",
    "Precision (predicted flops)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    task4_accuracy,
    task4_sensitivity,
    task4_specificity,
    task4_precision
  )
)

print(task4_metrics)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-threshold-comparison
#| include: false

# Compare classification results at two probability thresholds
task4_threshold_metrics <- function(threshold) {

  predicted <- ifelse(task4_predicted_prob >= threshold, 1L, 0L)

  actual <- task4_model_data$flop

  tp <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
  tn <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
  fp <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
  fn <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)

  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Accuracy = (tp + tn) / length(actual),
    Sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn),
    Specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
    Precision = tp / (tp + fp),
    Flops_Detected = tp,
    Flops_Missed = fn
  )
}

task4_threshold_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  task4_threshold_metrics(0.50),
  task4_threshold_metrics(0.30)
)

print(task4_threshold_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-classification-performance
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample classification performance at two probability thresholds."

task4_performance_display <- task4_threshold_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Threshold = paste0(round(Threshold * 100), "%"),
    dplyr::across(
      c(Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision),
      ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", .x * 100)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  task4_performance_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Threshold",
    "Accuracy",
    "Sensitivity",
    "Specificity",
    "Precision",
    "Flops detected",
    "Flops missed"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-confusion-matrix
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample confusion matrix at the 30% threshold."

task4_confusion_display <- table(
  Actual = factor(
    task4_model_data$flop,
    levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop")
  ),
  Predicted = factor(
    ifelse(task4_predicted_prob >= 0.30, 1, 0),
    levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop")
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(task4_confusion_display),
  col.names = c("Predicted non-flop", "Predicted flop")
)
```

**Classification performance**

At the standard 50% threshold, the model achieved 75.6% accuracy but identified only 5 of the 784 actual flops, giving a sensitivity of just 0.6%. Since flops represented approximately 24.4% of the modelling sample, predicting most films as non-flops produced a misleadingly high accuracy.

A 30% threshold was therefore considered more suitable for identifying financial risk. It increased sensitivity to 43.1%, correctly identifying 338 flops, although specificity decreased to 74.2% and precision was 35.0%. Overall accuracy fell to 66.6%.

For Meridian, identifying potentially unsuccessful productions before approval may be more valuable than maximising accuracy alone. However, the lower threshold also incorrectly flagged 627 non-flops, meaning these predictions should support further review rather than automatic rejection. The 30% threshold is a practical illustration of this trade-off, not a statistically proven optimum.

These results are based on the films used to fit the model and may overstate performance on future productions.

## Hypothetical Film Pitches

```{r}
#| label: task4-hypothetical-pitches
#| include: false

task4_pitches <- data.frame(
  Pitch = c(
    "Platform Zero",
    "The Meridian Protocol: Black Tide",
    "The Things We Never Recorded"
  ),
  primary_genre = c("Horror", "Action", "Drama"),
  franchise_status = c("Original", "Franchise", "Original"),
  budget_10m = c(0.9, 8.5, 1.8),
  crew_10 = c(2.4, 9, 3.8)
)

# Keep the same categories as the fitted model
task4_pitches$primary_genre <- factor(
  task4_pitches$primary_genre,
  levels = sort(unique(task4_model_data$primary_genre))
)

task4_pitches$franchise_status <- factor(
  task4_pitches$franchise_status,
  levels = levels(task4_model_data$franchise_status)
)

# Apply the standardisation used in the Bayesian model
task4_pitches <- task4_pitches |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    budget_z = (budget_10m - task4_budget_mean) / task4_budget_sd,
    crew_z = (crew_10 - task4_crew_mean) / task4_crew_sd
  )

print(task4_pitches)
```

```{r}
#| label: task4-pitch-predictions
#| include: false

# Build the predictor matrix using the fitted model's columns
task4_pitch_X <- model.matrix(
  ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + budget_z + crew_z,
  data = task4_pitches
)

# Ensure the columns match the Bayesian model
task4_pitch_X <- task4_pitch_X[, colnames(task4_mh_draws), drop = FALSE]

# Predicted flop probability for every posterior draw and pitch
task4_pitch_prob_draws <- plogis(
  task4_mh_draws %*% t(task4_pitch_X)
)

# Summarise the posterior probabilities
task4_pitch_results <- data.frame(
  Pitch = task4_pitches$Pitch,
  Median_Probability = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, median),
  Lower_95 = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025),
  Upper_95 = apply(task4_pitch_prob_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)
)

print(task4_pitch_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task4-pitch-predictions
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian predicted flop probabilities and 95% credible intervals for three hypothetical pitches."

task4_pitch_display <- task4_pitch_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Flop probability` = sprintf("%.1f%%", Median_Probability * 100),
    `95% credible interval` = sprintf(
      "%.1f%%–%.1f%%",
      Lower_95 * 100,
      Upper_95 * 100
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Pitch,
    `Flop probability`,
    `95% credible interval`
  )

knitr::kable(task4_pitch_display, row.names = FALSE)
```

### Greenlight recommendations

**The Meridian Protocol: Black Tide — Conditional greenlight**

This franchise action film has the lowest predicted flop probability at 4.7% (95% credible interval: 2.7%–7.9%). Although the estimated risk is relatively low, the proposed $85 million budget represents a substantial financial commitment. Meridian could move the project forward, provided the production budget and expected revenue are reviewed before final approval.

**Platform Zero — Conditional greenlight**

With a predicted flop probability of 16.0% (95% credible interval: 11.2%–22.2%), this original horror film presents a moderate level of risk compared with the other two pitches. Its $9 million budget makes it a smaller financial commitment. A conditional greenlight would allow Meridian to explore the project further while checking whether its expected audience and distribution plans support the investment.

**The Things We Never Recorded — Hold for further review**

This original drama has the highest predicted flop probability at 28.8% (95% credible interval: 25.6%–32.6%). Given its proposed $18 million budget, approving the project without further financial assessment would be difficult to justify. Meridian could review the budget, intended audience and distribution strategy before reconsidering the proposal.

These recommendations are based on estimated flop risk rather than guaranteed outcomes. A lower predicted probability does not necessarily mean a project offers a better financial return.

## Summary for the Head of Production

The greenlight model provides Meridian with an early assessment of a film's financial risk using information available before production begins. By considering genre, franchise status, budget and crew size, it estimates the likelihood of a film failing to recover its production budget.

Among the three proposed films, *The Meridian Protocol: Black Tide* has the lowest estimated flop risk, followed by *Platform Zero*. *The Things We Never Recorded* presents the greatest concern and would benefit from further review before approval.

However, the model has important limitations. Its predictions rely on historical films with sufficient financial information and do not capture factors such as audience demand, marketing, release timing or distribution arrangements. The model also estimates the chance of a flop, not the amount of money a studio might lose. Its classification results were assessed using the same films on which it was trained, so performance on future productions remains uncertain.

Meridian should therefore use these estimates as an early warning tool rather than a final decision-maker. Combining the model's findings with financial forecasts and professional judgement would provide a more balanced basis for greenlight decisions.
